title: Former Mexican goalkeeper charged in $5.4 million counterfeit watch trafficking scheme through Laredo
excerpt: Pedro Hernandez-Calderon, 45, a former professional goalkeeper for Atlas, Santos Laguna and Necaxa, is accused of running an import-export business that moved counterfeit luxury watches through Laredo to buyers in Mexico.
content:
A former professional soccer goalkeeper from Mexico has been charged in federal court in Laredo with trafficking in counterfeit goods, accused of moving counterfeit luxury watches through the city to customers in Mexico in a scheme federal prosecutors say was worth about $5.4 million.

Pedro Hernandez-Calderon, 45, a Mexican citizen, remains in custody pending further criminal proceedings, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. At his initial court appearance, prosecutors told the court he played goalkeeper for Mexican clubs Atlas, Santos Laguna and Necaxa.

According to the criminal complaint, the investigation began on October 5, when authorities in Anchorage, Alaska, seized four counterfeit luxury watches that were destined for a warehouse in Laredo. Authorities in Alaska coordinated with law enforcement in South Texas to identify those responsible, federal prosecutors said.

Prosecutors allege Hernandez-Calderon operated an import-export business that received counterfeit watches in Laredo for shipment to customers in Mexico. Between June 2025 and October 2026, authorities identified numerous shipments of counterfeit watches sent to Laredo addresses, with an estimated retail value of approximately $5.4 million if the watches had been genuine, according to the complaint.

Authorities also allegedly uncovered photographs, communications and shipping records documenting the operation, and representatives from luxury watch manufacturers confirmed the watches submitted for review were counterfeit, prosecutors said.

If convicted, Hernandez-Calderon faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a possible $2 million fine. Homeland Security Investigations led the investigation with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigations and the U.S. Postal Service, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Sekula is prosecuting the case.

A criminal complaint is a formal accusation, not evidence, and Hernandez-Calderon is presumed innocent unless convicted through due process of law.

Sources: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas (justice.gov); KGNS (kgns.tv).
